Syllabus

CSS 173 · Fundamentals of Programming Theory and Applications · Winter 2027draft

Vitals

  • Course Number and Title: CSS 173: Fundamentals of Programming Theory and Applications
  • Description: "Fundamental concepts and techniques for analysis, design and implementation of computer programming." Prerequisite: either CSS 142, CSE 122, or CSE 142. May not be repeated. (University of Washington Bothell, CSS course catalog, 2026–27)
  • Meeting Time/Place: Monday/Wednesday 5:45–7:45 PM, UW1 051. Section A, SLN 13199.
  • Prerequisites: See the prerequisites page, which has a self-check quiz.
  • Credit: 5 units. This translates into about 10 hours of work per week outside of class.
  • Notice: Contents of this Syllabus and the course web site can change at any time in the term.
  • Class Culture:
    • Excellence: I have high standards. You are expected to meet them.
    • Initiative: Ask questions! Engage and wrestle with the material, your colleagues, and myself.

Texts & Supplies

Course text (CT): chapters written for this course, on the course web site, one per topic. There is no book to buy.

Lecture files: each lecture is a Python file you download and run during class.

Computer requirements:

  • A laptop you can bring to every session (Windows, macOS, or Linux).
  • Python 3 and Visual Studio Code with the Python extension, both free. Installation instructions are posted before the first session.

What to bring: the laptop, and paper and a pen. Part of the work is done by hand.

Topics and Learning Objectives

Topics: Python as a calculator; functions and modules; plotting with Matplotlib; lists, tuples and loops; NumPy arrays and array syntax; basic statistics, correlation and lag autocorrelation; reading and writing text files; objects and exceptions; managing files and directories; searching a directory tree; recursion; classes and program design.

Learning Objectives: By the end of this course, students will:

  1. Design a program from a problem statement, using modular design, logic flow, data abstraction and pseudo-code.
  2. Write Python programs with the basic constructs, functions, and file input and output.
  3. Analyze a dataset: select, test and transform values with loops and with array syntax, compute statistics, and plot the results.
  4. Implement basic searching algorithms, including a recursive search of a directory tree.
  5. Automate file-management tasks: create, move, rename, copy and delete collections of files and directories.
  6. Test and debug a program as part of the development cycle.

Course Structure

Part Weeks Theme Core Question
I 1–6 Business Data Analysis What does this dataset say, and how do I compute it?
II 7–9 Automating and Managing Information Systems How do I make the computer do the filing?
III 10 Synthesis Can I carry an analysis from raw files to a presented result?

See the schedule for dates, readings, and due dates.

Requirements

Pre-Class Activities (PCA): Readings listed in the schedule are due before the session they are listed under. A PCA is a short Canvas quiz on the reading, due at the start of class.

In-Class Activities (ICA): Worksheets done during class and submitted on Canvas the same day.

Homework (HW): Eight assignments. Seven solve one data-analysis or file-management task each; the eighth is a dataset analysis project, presented in the last session. Homework is due at the start of class on its due date.

Programs that run: Your programs must run on a computer other than your own, with no absolute paths or other machine-specific settings.

Midterm: In class, 120 minutes.

Final Exam: In class, 120 minutes, cumulative, during the scheduled finals time.

Make-Up and Late Policy

Late tokens: Everyone has 2 late tokens for the term. A token extends one homework deadline by 48 hours. Tokens do not apply to pre-class activities, in-class activities, the project presentation, or exams. Without a token, late work is not accepted, and nothing is accepted after the last day of instruction, Fri Mar 12. Submit on Canvas, not by email.

Lowest score drops:

  • Pre-Class Activities: 2
  • In-Class Activities: 2

The drops cover a missed session without paperwork.

Exams: A missed exam is made up only for documented health issues, bereavement, university business, or legal obligations. Tell the instructor before the exam whenever possible.

Extra Credit

None.

AI Policy

AI tools may be used for learning, and for limited help on homework if you disclose it: cite the tool, summarize your prompts, and note any AI-assisted code in a comment. Using AI for a whole assignment is misconduct, and AI is not allowed during quizzes or exams. If you used none, say so: "I did not use any AI tools for this assignment."

Collaboration & Academic Integrity

Guidelines:

  • For homework: You may discuss approaches with classmates. The code and the write-up you submit are your own.
  • For in-class activities: Work with your group; submit your own copy.
  • For quizzes and exams: Individual work only.

Internet and programming resources:

  • Small snippets: attribute if non-obvious
  • Substantial blocks: must cite source and mark copied lines
  • Ideas from other code: attribute non-obvious ideas
  • Copyrighted code: note in comments; do not distribute without permission

Due process: Suspected violations are referred under the UW Student Conduct Code, which describes your rights and the appeal process.
